title: An AI factor-mining agent found this order-flow signal. I put $10k behind it for 28 days. What would you try to break first?
author: Rare_Inflation3178
selftext:
**Title:**  
An AI agent mined this crypto order-flow signal. I tested it with $10k for 28 days. What would you try to break first?  
**Body:**  
I’ve been building an AI-assisted workflow for researching, validating, and monitoring systematic crypto strategies.  
This order-flow signal was originally discovered by the factor-mining agent. The agent translated a research hypothesis into a candidate factor and implemented the signal logic, but it still had to pass a series of validation checks before I was willing to test it with real capital.  
I started running it with a $10,000 account on July 1.  
After 28 realized days:  
• Net return: +6.49%  
• Maximum drawdown: 1.73%  
• Positive days: 18 out of 28  
• Starting capital: $10,000  
• Strategy changes after launch: zero  
The entry logic, exits, filters, and position-sizing rules were fixed before the test began. I haven’t changed the strategy based on the live results.  
The return shown is after actual exchange fees. This is real capital, but it’s still a small account and a very short test window, so I’m not claiming durable alpha.  
The part I find more interesting isn’t whether an AI agent can produce a profitable-looking signal. It’s whether an AI-assisted workflow can:  
Reject weak signals before deployment  
Identify which assumptions are breaking after deployment  
Suggest useful diagnostics without repeatedly rewriting the strategy until the equity curve looks good  
The main failure modes I’m looking at now are:  
• Returns concentrated in a small number of trades  
• Dependence on the current market regime  
• Cross-asset or trading-session concentration  
• Slippage and adverse selection under changing volatility  
• Capacity limits as position size increases  
• A lucky 28-day window rather than a persistent signal  
For people using AI in systematic trading, where do you think the AI is actually most useful: generating hypotheses, implementing signals, validating them, or monitoring degradation?  
And looking at this result specifically, what would you try to break first?  
For context, this signal came from the factor-mining agent inside my workflow, a validation workflow I’m building. I’m currently testing it with three traders and can include a few more beta users who already research or run systematic crypto strategies.  
If that sounds relevant, comment with what you trade and how you currently validate signals. No need to reveal the strategy itself.

comments.author: AutomaticPayment9480
comments.body:
Orderflow is going to need context , one signal can mean multiple things depending on the regime. Ai is useful in the right context as well. If you give it the necessary data it should take you where you want to go. Not sure what you mean by breaking, this doesn’t really give a lot of info and unless it’s crypto it’s only 20 days of trading. 
How many trades is it taking a session? What about commission? That right there can knock you back a few steps.

replies.author: Rare_Inflation3178
replies.body:
Good questions.  
It’s crypto, so that’s 28 calendar days rather than 20 trading days.  
This isn’t a high-frequency bot taking a fixed number of trades. It’s a daily rebalanced cross-sectional portfolio, so turnover is the metric I care about more than trade count.  
The returns already include a 7 bp per side transaction cost. I haven’t modeled market impact or capacity yet, so those are still open questions.  
By “break it,” I mean finding where the edge disappears: different volatility regimes, liquidity conditions, delayed execution, higher costs, concentration, larger position sizes, etc.  
I completely agree on the context point. My hesitation is that every regime filter makes the model more complex, so I’m trying to figure out which ones improve robustness versus just fitting history.  
If you had to add just one contextual filter, what would it be?

replies.author: AutomaticPayment9480
replies.body:
Momentum imo is probably the best, that way if your entry isn’t great you can still get rewarded. 

My algo has a volatitlity engime, regime engine, volume engine, delta engine, price action engine, level state engine, rejection engine,zone engine, i got a lotta engines lol. 

Reading orderflow has been extremely tricky for me, it took months for me to actually get on the right side of data. Im using volume by price and delta by price for my control engine. But it needs a lot of context to analyze the metrics, thats where he level state and rejection engine, i also have trend engine and my volume engine for price and volume migration for detecting regime change along with my consolation tracker to track price in a rotation. I still think momentum is probably the strongest and if you can read momentum correctly , paired with orderflow, thats a strong system.

replies.author: Rare_Inflation3178
replies.body:
Yeah, that makes sense. Momentum is probably the first thing I’d test too. Do you use it as a hard filter, or just to change position size/direction?  
Also curious how you keep all those engines from turning into one giant overfit machine lol.

replies.author: AutomaticPayment9480
replies.body:
The engines just compute the raw data. Then you use that data to orchestrate the session behavior. Its a lot for sure, but you need to be able to detect volatility, liquidity, regime, rejection at a minimum. Being blind to one of those can harm entry/exit logic. 

Im not really sure what you mean by filter, i dont use filters so i honestly cant answer that question but you can do two different things you can measure momentum as a percentage or you can have a multi stage process that can detect different levels of momentum with direction. My algo uses a state machine to analyze the market behavior.
